# Results — Study 793 (Cross-sectional commodity value)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The claim under test —
**Asness, Moskowitz & Pedersen (2013), the commodity value leg: rank a commodity basket on
the ratio of the price ~5 years ago to the current price; the cheap (fallen) commodities
outperform the expensive (risen) ones.** Offline & deterministic once cached; run
`python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number. As-of **2026-06-30** (the last
complete calendar month; the partial current month is dropped). Fingerprint `0524773df8ac`
(raw daily closes, the value-signal input).*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily closes for the **same 13 liquid single-commodity ETFs** as sibling 792 — GLD SLV PPLT PALL CPER (metals), USO UNG UGA (energy), CORN WEAT SOYB CANE DBA (ags) — 5,406 rows, 2005-01-03 → 2026-06-30. **Raw** close (`auto_adjust=False`) for the value signal; **total-return** (adjusted) close for the P&L |
| Value signal | **AMP 5-year value**: `log(P_ref) − log(P_t)`, where `P_ref` is the average price over the ~4.5–5.5-years-ago band (a 13-month window centred 60 months before *t*) and `P_t` is the current price. **Positive = price fell = cheap = long.** Measured on the *raw price level* (not total return), so five years of carry/roll do not masquerade as value |
| Monthly panels | price panel 258 month-ends (2005-01 → 2026-06); return panel 220 month-ends. The cross-sectional L/S trades **163 months, 2012-12-31 → 2026-06-30**, once ≥ 6 names carry a full 5-year price history |
| Portfolio | long the top third (cheapest/fallen), short the bottom third (most expensive/risen), equal-weight each leg (1× long / 1× short = gross 2× NAV, dollar-neutral) |
| Execution | one documented lag — weights formed at the close of month *t* earn the return of month *t*+1 (a single `shift`, applied once) |
| Costs | one-way cost × traded notional (turnover = Σ\|Δw\|); the short leg pays borrow at 50 bps/yr on its 1× NAV |
| Statistics | **HAC/Newey-West t** (Bartlett, automatic lag) on the monthly L/S mean is the decisive stat; one-sample t + annualised Sharpe alongside; a 40-seed random-rank placebo; a sub-period contrast tested as a difference |

**Survivorship is named on the Signal axis.** The basket is *current* membership. For a
*value* (buy-the-fallen) sleeve the bias points **for** the effect: a fund that fell far
enough to delist is a "deep value" name that never mean-reverted, and its absence flatters
the cheap/long leg — so any value premium here is an **upper bound**. **Roll-contamination
is also named:** for chronic-contango energy ETFs (USO, UNG, UGA) even the raw price grinds
down for years, so they read as perennially "cheap" for a mechanical reason unrelated to a
value reversal; the ETF proxy cannot separate spot value from roll drift the way AMP's spot
series can.

## The headline — 5-year value L/S (long cheap, short expensive)

| quantity | value |
|---|--:|
| mean monthly L/S return (n=163) | **+8.05 bps** (~**+0.97%/yr**) |
| **HAC/Newey-West t** (4 lags) | **+0.166** ← decisive, **far below the t ≥ 2 bar** |
| one-sample t | +0.180 |
| annualised Sharpe | **+0.049** |
| hit rate (months > 0) | 54.0% |
| avg one-way turnover | 0.31× NAV / month |

The point estimate is economically nil (~+1%/yr gross, Sharpe 0.05) and the
autocorrelation-robust statistic — the one the desk certifies on — is **t = 0.17**, a flat
zero. **On this investable ETF tape the commodity value leg simply is not there.**

## Leg decomposition (excess-of-basket) — do the cheap names actually bounce?

| leg | excess vs equal-weight basket | HAC t |
|---|--:|--:|
| cheap (long) leg | **−9.88 bps/mo** | −0.32 |
| expensive (short) leg | +17.93 bps/mo | +0.69 |
| equal-weight basket | +1.29%/yr | — |

The direction check is the punchline: the **cheap (fallen) leg actually *lost* to the
basket** (−9.88 bps/mo) — the opposite of the value prediction. What little the L/S made
came entirely from the *short* (expensive) side, and even that is noise (t = 0.69). The
"fallen commodities bounce back" story is **not just weak here — it points the wrong way.**

## Random-rank placebo — is the sort better than noise?

Replace the value signal with i.i.d. noise ranks (breadth held fixed via the real signal's
live mask), rebuild the same L/S book, **40 seeds**:

| quantity | value |
|---|--:|
| real HAC t | +0.166 |
| placebo mean HAC t (sd) | +0.222 (1.109) |
| placebo mean Sharpe | +0.059 |
| placebos with \|t\| ≥ 2 | 3 / 40 (8%) |
| p(placebo t ≥ real t) | **0.525** |

The real value sort is **indistinguishable from a coin-flip ranking** — in fact the *median*
random rank did marginally better (placebo mean t 0.22 > real 0.17), p = 0.53. There is no
signal to certify.

## Sub-period contrast — was there ever a value premium here?

Split at **2019-07-01** (≈ the effective-sample midpoint):

| era | mean/mo | HAC t | Sharpe |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 2012-12 → 2019-06 (n=79) | +20.92 bps | +0.33 | +0.14 |
| 2019-07 → 2026-06 (n=84) | −4.05 bps | −0.06 | −0.02 |
| Welch t of the difference (late − early) | | −0.28 | |

Neither half carries a premium (both HAC t well under 1); the difference is noise
(Welch t = −0.28). This is not a *faded* effect — it is one that was **never certifiable on
this tape in either half.**

## The costed timer — one-way × NAV, short leg pays borrow

| cost (one-way/side) | gross | net | net HAC t | net Sharpe | turnover |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 5 bps | +0.97%/yr | **+0.28%/yr** | +0.05 | 0.01 | 0.31× |
| 10 bps | +0.97%/yr | **+0.09%/yr** | +0.02 | 0.00 | 0.31× |

Turnover is low (0.31× NAV — a 5-year signal barely moves), so costs are not the issue; the
gross was already ~zero. Net is a rounding error either way. There is nothing to trade.

## Synthetic positive control — the machinery works

Deterministic monthly **price** panel; prices follow a log random walk whose next return
carries a drift = `val_edge` × (log price ~5y ago − log price now), so fallen names are
pushed back up (genuine long-horizon reversal). No network.

| world | 5-year value L/S HAC t |
|---|--:|
| null (`val_edge` = 0, random walk), **20 seeds** | mean **−0.23** (sd 0.97), \|t\| ≥ 2 in **2/20** seeds |
| planted (`val_edge` = 0.05, seed 793) | **+6.41** (+257 bps/mo, Sharpe 1.98) |

The detector is **unbiased** (null mean t ≈ 0) and lights up strongly on a planted reversal.
It clears \|t\| = 2 on ~2/20 null seeds — the false-positive rate you expect from noise,
which is *why* a synthetic control can never certify a real-tape stamp; it only proves the
sort *can* find value when value is there. On the real tape it reads 0.17 — the machinery is
fine; **the effect is absent.** *(A machinery / power check only — never cited in support of
the real-tape stamp.)*

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** The 5-year value L/S earns **+8 bps/mo (~+1%/yr, Sharpe 0.05)** with
  **HAC t = +0.17 — a flat zero**, indistinguishable from a random-rank sort (placebo
  *p* = 0.53), and the *cheap (long) leg actually underperforms the basket* (−9.88 bps/mo).
  The AMP claim is real in a broad spot-futures cross-section; **on this investable
  13-ETF tape it is absent — and the survivorship + roll caveats mean these numbers are an
  upper bound.**
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** Net is ~0%/yr at any realistic cost (net HAC t ≈ 0). There is no
  edge to capture; low turnover is irrelevant when the gross is already zero.
- **Do fallen commodities bounce? — REFUTED (on this tape).** The long (cheap) leg's excess
  return is *negative* (−9.88 bps/mo, t = −0.32). Over 2012-2026 the fallen single-commodity
  ETFs did not out-bounce the risen ones — if anything the reverse.
